'''Robert Heinz Abeles''' (January 14, 1926 – June 18, 2000) was an American biochemist, dedicated in particular to enzymology and chemical biology.<ref name = walsh>{{cite journal | journal = Proc. Amer. Philosoph. Soc. |volume = 151|number = 3|year = 2007|author = Christopher T. Walsh|pages = 331–335 | title = Robert Heinz Abeles}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |journal= Trends Biochem. Sci. | volume = 26|number = 1| title = Robert H. Abeles (1926–2000) |pages = 74–75 | last1 = Stubbe | first1 = JoAnne | last2 = Ringe|first2 = Dagmar|year =2001| doi = 10.1016/S0968-0004(00)01736-9}}</ref><ref name = nature>{{cite journal | journal= Nature| title = Robert H. Abeles (1926–2000) | last1 = Hedstrom | first1 = Lizbeth|last2 = Frey | first2 = Perry A. | year = 2000 | pages = 854| volume = 407| issue = 6806 | doi = 10.1038/35038202 | pmid = 11057653 | s2cid = 204470254 | doi-access = free }}</ref> He was born in Vienna, but his family moved to Chicago in 1939, and he made most of his career at [[Brandeis University]]. In his later years, Abeles had serious health problems, including Hodgkin's disease in the 1970s and Parkinson's disease in the last ten years.<ref name = nature />

==Education==
After undergraduate studies at the [[University of Chicago]], and doctoral work at the [[University of Colorado]], Abeles carried out post-doctoral research under the supervision of [[Frank Westheimer]] in the chemistry department at [[Harvard University]]. This research formed the starting point for his life's work on the mechanisms of the chemical reactions of living systems.<ref name = walsh />

==Ohio State, Michigan and Brandeis==
After faculty appointments at [[Ohio State University]] and the [[University of Michigan]], moved in 1964 to the recently inaugurated department of biochemistry at Brandeis, and remained there for 36 years, until he died in 2000. He and [[William Jencks]] together turned Brandeis into a leading center in the world for chemical biochemistry.<ref name = walsh />

==Research==
Abeles, together with Jencks and Westheimer, fostered a strong belief that chemical mechanisms could explain all aspects of metabolism.<ref name = walsh />

With Alan Maycock, Abeles carried out important work on [[Suicide inhibition|suicide enzyme inactivators]],<ref>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1021/ar50105a001|journal = Acc. Chem. Res.| volume = 9|number = 9|pages = 313–319 | year = 1976|first1 = R. H. |last1 = Abeles|first2 = A. L.|last2 = Maycock| title = suicide enzyme inactivators}}</ref> using their expertise to design inactivators of γ-cystathionase,<ref>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1021/ja00799a053|title = Acetylenic enzyme inactivators: inactivation of γ-cystathionase, ''in vitro'' and ''in vivo'', by propargylglycine|journal = J. Amer. Chem. Soc.|first1 = R. H. |last1 = Abeles|first2 =C. T. | last2 = Walsh| year=1973 |volume = 95|number = 18 | pages = 6124–6125| pmid=4733835}}</ref> and other enzymes.

==Awards==
Abeles was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1999,<ref name = walsh /> and inducted into the Medicinal Chemistry Hall of Fame of the [[American Chemical Society]].<ref name = walsh /> He received the [[Welch Award in Chemistry]] in 1995.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://welch1.org/awards/welch-award-in-chemistry/past-recipients|title = Past Recipients}}</ref>
